q-28529.name: Question 1
q-28529.problem:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{1}{8}(x+4)(x+2)^{2}?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-28529.worked_solution:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=-4$ and a double root at $x=-2.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{8}(0+4)(0+2)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(4)(2)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(4)(4) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,2),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-4,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/021fddfcb24a74f7ed6ce4007561844375089b81c3aa1d6a42b6da9dc769df90.png)

q-112145.name: Question 3
q-112145.problem:
Given that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x)={x}^{3}-4{x}^{2}-3x+18,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(*Note: Figures not drawn to scale*)
q-112145.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -4 & -3 & 18 \\  &  & -2 & 12 & -18 \\  & 1 & -6 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x+2}={x}^{2}-6x+9
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x+2)({x}^{2}-6x+9).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=(x+2)(x-3)(x-3)=(x+2)(x-3)^{2}.
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=-2$ and a double root at $x=3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0+2)(0-3)^{2} \\  & =(2)(-3)^{2} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,18),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=3.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/266609da7c307b98b8d5f280c75f6d8fd557c23b2e2e1885be37fa4ee3d7b229.png)

q-112137.name: Question 4
q-112137.problem:

$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{f(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}-5x+4
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}-5x+4).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=(x-1)(x-1)(x-4)=(x-4)(x-1)^{2}.
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=4$ and a double root at $x=1.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =(0-4)(0-1)^{2} \\  & =(-4)(-1)^{2} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,-4),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=4,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=1.$

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

q-75155.name: Question 5
q-75155.problem: Which of the following curves is generated by $y=\frac{1}{3}(2-x)(3+x)^{2}?$
q-75155.worked_solution:
The equation is already in factored form, so by the zero-product rule, we deduce that it has a single root at $x=2$ and a double root at $x=-3.$ 

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{1}{3}(2-0)(3+0)^{2} \\  & =\frac{(2)(3)^{2}}{3} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,6),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-3.$

Notice that the leading coefficient is *negative*:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{3}(2-x)(3+x)^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2-x)({x}^{2}+6x+9) \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

q-75165.name: Question 7
q-75165.problem:
Given that $x-4$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}+10{x}^{2}-32x+32$, which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

*(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)*
q-75165.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-4)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 4 & -1 & 10 & -32 & 32 \\  &  & -4 & 24 & -32 \\  & -1 & 6 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x-4} & =-{x}^{2}+6x-8 \\  & =-({x}^{2}-6x+8)\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
f(x)=-(x-4)({x}^{2}-6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=-(x-4)(x-2)(x-4)=-(x-2)(x-4)^{2}
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=2$ and a double root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-2)(0-4)^{2} \\  & =-(-2)(-4)^{2} \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,32),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=2,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=4.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14238854/assets/aae66bc5dcf29e5e85e33942541b510d136b4f7f13d633f28c46d4b5a9ca977b.png)

q-112166.name: Question 8
q-112166.problem:
Given that $x+2$ is a factor of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+8x+12,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

*(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)*
q-112166.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+2)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+2)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+2)$ using synthetic division:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & -1 & -1 & 8 & 12 \\  &  & 2 & -2 & -12 \\  & -1 & 1 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(x)}{x+2} & =-{x}^{2}+x+6\end{aligned}
$$

which means that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+2)(-{x}^{2}+x+6) \\  & =-(x+2)({x}^{2}-x-6).\end{aligned}
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
f(x)=-(x+2)(x+2)(x-3)=-(x-3)(x+2)^{2}.
$$

Now that we have the cubic in factored form, we can tell that it has a single root at $x=3$ and a double root at $x=-2.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-(0-3)(0+2)^{2} \\  & =-(-3)(2)^{2} \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the curve

- intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,12),$

- passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

- touches the $x$-axis and turns around at the double root $x=-2.$

Because the leading coefficient is negative, the graph takes an $\text{S}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:
